blocks.html: A note for parents: Lucretius argues that the soul does not survive death and that the gods take no part in the world; these are his views, presented as his. Book IV includes a frank passage on love, and Book VI ends with a grim account of a plague; the lesson leaves out both.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

About 2,080 years ago, a Roman poet named Lucretius wrote a long poem with a big idea: everything in the world is made of tiny bits, far too small to see, that are always moving. He called them the "first-beginnings" of things. We call them atoms.

How could he know about things nobody could see? He used clues. Wet clothes dry in the sun, but you never see the water leave. A stone step wears down over many years, but you never see a single bit go. So, he said, the bits must be too small to see.

blocks.name: gb-atoms
blocks.cap: Watch the black speck get knocked about by tiny moving bodies. Then hide them: the speck still wanders.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A smell race. Have someone open a jar of something with a strong smell, like an orange peel or vanilla, at one end of a room. Stand at the other end and time how long until you smell it. Nothing visible crossed the room. What did? Lucretius would say: tiny bodies, moving through the air.

Lucretius also noticed dust dancing in a sunbeam in a dark room, and thought invisible bodies were knocking it about. Today we know the dust is mostly pushed by moving air, but very tiny specks seen under a microscope really are jiggled by bumping molecules. That jiggling helped prove atoms exist, about 1,950 years after Lucretius wrote.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–c. 55 BC) lived in the last years of the Roman Republic, a time of civil wars. Almost nothing is known of his life. His one work, On the Nature of Things (De rerum natura), is a poem in six books. The orator Cicero mentions it in a letter of 54 BC, praising both its brilliance and its skill.

Lucretius followed the Greek philosopher Epicurus (341–270 BC), who taught that the aim of life is peace of mind, and that the greatest threats to it are fear of the gods and fear of death. Lucretius's problem was how to free his readers from those fears. His answer was physics: if people understood that everything happens by natural causes, he argued, they would stop being afraid. These are Lucretius's own views about religion and death; readers, religious and not, have long argued with them.

Lucretius's two first principles: nothing comes from nothing, and nothing is ever destroyed into nothing. Everything is made of atoms, which can't be created or destroyed, moving in empty space (the void).

blocks.text: Evidence for bodies you can't see

blocks.html: This is a good argument from evidence: we see the total loss, so something must be leaving, but each piece is too small to see. It still works. A gold ring worn every day for fifty years loses a measurable amount of gold, a few atoms at a time.

blocks.title: How small?
blocks.q: Suppose a gold ring loses 0.06 grams over 30 years of wear. A gram of gold has about $3 \times 10^{21}$ atoms. About how many atoms leave each second?
steps: Atoms lost: $0.06 \times 3 \times 10^{21} = 1.8 \times 10^{20}$.
Seconds in 30 years: $30 \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600 \approx 9.5 \times 10^{8}$.
Per second: $1.8 \times 10^{20} \div 9.5 \times 10^{8} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{11}$, about 200 billion atoms every second, and still you can't see the ring change from day to day.

blocks.name: gb-atoms
blocks.cap: A large speck among many small moving bodies. Hide the small ones and watch the speck wander.

blocks.html: Saying Lucretius discovered Brownian motion. The dust in a sunbeam is moved mostly by air currents, not by single molecules; it is far too big. The real effect was seen by the botanist Robert Brown in 1827, watching pollen grains' tiny particles under a microscope. Einstein explained it mathematically in 1905, and Jean Perrin's measurements of 1908 convinced nearly all scientists that atoms are real. Lucretius had the right idea for the wrong example.

blocks.title: A random walk
blocks.q: A speck is knocked one tiny step in a random direction each time. On average, how far from its start is it after 100 steps of 1 micrometer? After 400?
steps: For a random walk, the typical distance grows as the square root of the number of steps.
After 100 steps: $\sqrt{100} \times 1 = 10$ micrometers.
After 400 steps: $\sqrt{400} \times 1 = 20$ micrometers. Four times the steps, only twice the distance.

items: Book II: atoms come in many shapes but not infinitely many; they fall through the void and sometimes "swerve" slightly, which Lucretius uses to explain free will.
Book III: the mind and spirit are made of very fine atoms and do not survive death, so death, he argues, is nothing to fear.
Book IV: how we see, hear and dream.
Book V: how the world, life and human society began, including an early picture of living things that failed to survive because they were not fitted to their surroundings.
Book VI: thunder, earthquakes, volcanoes, magnets and disease.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: conservation (Lavoisier, 1789, showed that mass is neither created nor destroyed in chemical change); atoms (Dalton, 1808); and the habit of explaining the visible by the invisible.
Changed: atoms are not indivisible. The electron was found in 1897 and the nucleus in 1911. And they are not tiny hooked or smooth pellets, as Lucretius pictured.

Wrong: following Epicurus, Lucretius said the Sun is about as big as it looks, and he rejected the idea that things fall toward a center, which led him to deny that people could live on the other side of a round Earth.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

By the Middle Ages the poem had nearly vanished. In 1417 the Italian book hunter Poggio Bracciolini found a copy in a German monastery and had it copied. Printed in 1473, it was read by Montaigne (later on this ladder), who quotes it often; by the philosopher Pierre Gassendi, who revived atomism in the 1600s; and by Thomas Jefferson, who owned several copies. Scientists of the 1600s such as Boyle and Newton built on an atomism that owed much to Epicurus and Lucretius, though they put it within a world made by God.

Some recent writers have claimed that this one rediscovery started the modern world. Many historians think that goes too far: the scientific revolution had many causes. But the poem was one of the routes by which ancient atomism reached early modern science.

Lucretius believed that understanding nature brings calm. Many readers since have shared some version of that hope; others have argued that his picture of a purposeless world leaves something out. Dante, Milton and Pascal, later on this ladder, offer very different accounts. The question of what science can and cannot tell us about how to live is one the Great Books keep returning to.

items: Is it reasonable to believe in things nobody can see? What evidence would convince you?
Lucretius thought knowing the causes of things would take away fear. Does understanding something make it less frightening?
A poem taught science for centuries. Can poetry teach science well?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Do the smell race. How else could you show that tiny invisible things are moving around you?
  2. Lucretius said nothing comes from nothing. Can you think of anything that seems to come from nothing? Where does it really come from?
  3. When a log burns, it seems to disappear. Where does it go?
  4. Why do you think Lucretius wrote about science as a poem instead of a plain book?
  5. Lucretius was right about atoms but for some wrong reasons. Is it still fair to give him credit?

Lucretius, Of the Nature of Things, verse translation by William Ellery Leonard (1916), Project Gutenberg

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Nicomachus lived about 1,900 years ago in Gerasa, a Roman city in what is now Jordan. He wrote a short book about the personalities of numbers: which are even and which odd, which can be split into equal rows, and which are special in other ways.
Some numbers make pictures. Put dots in rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 and you get a triangle of 10 dots. Make rows of 3, 3 and 3 and you get a square of 9. Nicomachus called these triangular and square numbers.

blocks.name: gb-figurate
blocks.cap: Pick a kind and slide n to grow the picture.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Dots and beans. With dried beans or pennies, build the triangles for 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15. Put two triangles side by side: what shape do you get? Now build squares 1, 4, 9 and 16. How many beans do you add each time to go from one square to the next? (Try the odd numbers.)

Nicomachus also liked perfect numbers. The numbers that divide 6 evenly, apart from 6, are 1, 2 and 3. Add them: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. The number is exactly the sum of its parts! The next perfect number is 28. They are rare: there are only four below 10,000.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Nicomachus (c. AD 60–c. 120) came from Gerasa, a prosperous city of the Roman province of Syria (today Jerash in Jordan). He was a Pythagorean: a follower of the old tradition, going back to Pythagoras in the 500s BC, that saw number as the key to music, the heavens and the order of the world. He also wrote a short handbook on music theory.

His problem was teaching. Euclid had proved results about numbers, but his Elements are hard going. Nicomachus wrote an introduction for students: definitions, names and many worked examples, with no proofs. It became one of the most copied textbooks in history. Boethius adapted it into Latin around AD 500, and his version was the standard arithmetic of European schools for about a thousand years, as the first of the four mathematical arts (arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy). Thabit ibn Qurra translated it into Arabic in the 800s.

head: Name
Meaning
Examples
rows: keeps halving evenly all the way down to 1
halves once to an odd number
halves more than once, but not down to 1
an odd number measured only by the unit
an odd number with another odd factor
blocks.cap: Nicomachus's names for kinds of numbers (Book I). He treats 2 as even-times even and lists primes among the odd numbers.

blocks.html: To find the odd primes he describes the method Eratosthenes, the librarian of Alexandria, had called the sieve. Nicomachus's book is our earliest surviving description of it.

blocks.title: Sifting to 50
blocks.q: Use the sieve to find the odd primes below 50.
steps: Write the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, …, 49.
Cross out every third one after 3 (9, 15, 21, 27, 33, 39, 45): the multiples of 3.
Cross out the multiples of 5 after 5 (25, 35); 15 and 45 are already gone.
Cross out the multiples of 7 after 7 (49; 21 and 35 are gone). Since $7 \times 7 = 49$ is the last square below 50, we can stop.

blocks.text: Too much, too little and just right

blocks.html: Nicomachus sorts numbers by adding up their parts (the smaller numbers that divide them exactly). If the parts add to less than the number, it is deficient; if more, superabundant; if exactly equal, perfect.

blocks.name: gb-perfect
blocks.cap: Each number is colored by whether its parts fall short, overshoot or land exactly. Press one to see its parts.

blocks.html: He gives the first four perfect numbers, 6, 28, 496 and 8,128, and a recipe for making more that is Euclid's IX.36 in other words: add 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … and, whenever the sum is prime, multiply it by the last number added.

Trusting every pattern Nicomachus states. He says there is one perfect number among the units, one among the tens, one among the hundreds and one among the thousands, and that they end alternately in 6 and 8. Both patterns fail. The fifth perfect number, 33,550,336, has eight digits, so there is none with five, six or seven; and the fifth and sixth (8,589,869,056) both end in 6. He saw the pattern in four examples and did not prove it. That is the difference between his book and Euclid's.

blocks.name: gb-figurate
blocks.cap: Triangular, square, pentagonal and oblong numbers, and the cubes built from odd numbers.

blocks.html: Book II arranges numbers as shapes made of points: polygonal numbers (triangular, square, pentagonal, …), oblong numbers (a side times one more: 2, 6, 12, 20), and solid numbers like pyramids and cubes. Along the way come neat facts: every square is the sum of two neighboring triangular numbers, and if you add the odd numbers in groups (1; 3 + 5; 7 + 9 + 11; …) you get the cubes 1, 8, 27, …

blocks.title: The cube of 4 from odd numbers
blocks.q: Which odd numbers add up to $4^3$ in Nicomachus's pattern?
steps: Groups so far: 1 | 3, 5 | 7, 9, 11. The fourth group takes the next four odd numbers.
They are 13, 15, 17 and 19.

blocks.title: Three kinds of mean
blocks.q: Find the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of 4 and 9 (where they are whole numbers).
steps: Arithmetic mean: halfway, $\frac{4 + 9}{2} = 6.5$.
Geometric mean: the number $g$ with $4 : g = g : 9$, so $g^2 = 36$, $g = 6$.
Harmonic mean: $\frac{2 \times 4 \times 9}{4 + 9} = \frac{72}{13} \approx 5.54$. Only the geometric mean is a whole number here.

blocks.html: The book ends with ten kinds of proportion. Nicomachus calls 6, 8, 9, 12 the "most perfect proportion": 9 is the arithmetic mean of 6 and 12, 8 is their harmonic mean, and the ratios 6 : 8 and 9 : 12 (3 : 4), 6 : 9 and 8 : 12 (2 : 3), and 6 : 12 (1 : 2) are the musical intervals of the fourth, the fifth and the octave.

blocks.text: What later mathematics kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the sieve, figurate numbers, perfect and abundant numbers, and the means. Mathematicians still use the words abundant and deficient.
Dropped: the moral and religious meanings Nicomachus gave to numbers, such as calling equality the source of goodness. Those belong to his Pythagorean philosophy, not to arithmetic.

Changed: arithmetic since Fermat and Euler rests on proofs, not examples. The questions Nicomachus raised are still open in places: no one knows whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers, or any odd ones.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Nicomachus and Euclid cover some of the same ground, the kinds of numbers and the recipe for perfect numbers, but they work in different ways. Euclid proves each claim from definitions. Nicomachus shows examples, names the patterns and leaves it there. For teaching beginners his way has strengths: students see and count before they prove. But it lets mistakes in, as with his patterns for perfect numbers.

This is a lasting question in teaching mathematics: how much should beginners see and count, and how soon should they meet proofs? The medieval schools learned from Boethius's Nicomachus for centuries before Euclid's proofs came back into wide use.

For Nicomachus, number was the pattern in the mind of the maker of the world, and arithmetic was the first of the sciences because the others depend on it. Readers today can take or leave that philosophy, but the practical point survived: music is ratios of string lengths, astronomy is cycles and periods, and geometry needs measurement. Kepler, Galileo and Newton, later on this ladder, kept the conviction that nature is written in numbers, while dropping the number mysticism.

items: Is a pattern that holds for four examples likely to hold forever? How many examples would convince you?
Why do people give personalities and meanings to numbers (lucky numbers, unlucky numbers)?
Nicomachus's book was read for 1,000 years. What makes a textbook last?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Build the first five triangular numbers with beans. What do you add each time?
  2. Do you have a favorite number? What is special about it: is it even, odd, prime, square, triangular?
  3. Nicomachus guessed a pattern from four perfect numbers and was wrong. When have you guessed a pattern that turned out to break?
  4. Why might a teacher show examples first and proofs later? Is that how you like to learn?
  5. Nicomachus thought numbers explained music. Can you find the 1 : 2 ratio by plucking a string, then pressing it down at its middle?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Ptolemy was an astronomer who lived in Alexandria, in Egypt, about 1,900 years ago. He wrote a giant book that explained how to predict where the Sun, the Moon and the planets would be in the sky, years ahead. People used it for about 1,400 years.

Ptolemy thought the Earth stood still in the middle, with everything else going around it. The tricky part was the planets. Mars, for example, usually drifts slowly eastward against the stars, night after night. But every two years or so it slows down, goes backward for a few weeks, then turns forward again!

Ptolemy explained this with a circle on a circle. Mars rides around a small circle, and the center of the small circle rides around a big circle. When Mars is on the inside of its small circle, it seems to go backward.

blocks.name: gb-epicycle
blocks.cap: Watch Mars loop backward. Then switch to the Sun in the middle and see the same thing another way.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Act it out. You need two people and a lamp for the Sun. One person (Earth) walks a small circle around the lamp; the other (Mars) walks a bigger circle, more slowly. Earth keeps pointing at Mars. When Earth overtakes Mars on the inside, Earth's arm swings backward for a while, though both are still walking forward. That is the backward loop!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Claudius Ptolemy (c. AD 100–c. 170) worked in Alexandria under Roman rule. His observations date from AD 127 to 141. He called his great work the Mathematical Composition; Arabic translators called it al-majisti, "the greatest", which became Almagest in Latin. He also wrote major books on geography, optics, music theory and astrology.

The problem he faced was prediction. Greek astronomers had believed for centuries that heavenly motions must be built from uniform circles. Hipparchus (c. 190–c. 120 BC) had made this work for the Sun and Moon, but his books are lost. Nobody had produced a full, working theory for the planets, with tables anyone could use to compute their positions. Ptolemy did.

No public-domain English translation of the Almagest exists, so this lesson describes it in our own words, with no quotations. The standard English translation is G. J. Toomer's (1984); the Great Books set uses R. Catesby Taliaferro's (1952). Both are under copyright. Look for them in a library.

head: Books
Subject
rows: The heavens are a sphere and turn as one; the Earth is a sphere at the center, motionless, and tiny compared with the distance to the stars. A table of chords (an early form of trigonometry).
The Sun's motion and the length of the year.
The Moon, and the distances of the Sun and Moon.
Eclipses of the Sun and Moon.
The fixed stars: a catalog of 1,022 stars in 48 constellations, with positions and brightness on a scale of six magnitudes.
The five planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.

blocks.html: For each planet Ptolemy used a big circle, the deferent, around the Earth, and a small circle, the epicycle, whose center rides along the deferent. The planet moves on the epicycle. When the planet is on the near side of its epicycle, moving opposite to the epicycle's center, it appears to move backward: retrograde motion.

blocks.name: gb-epicycle
blocks.cap: Change the epicycle's size. With no epicycle there are no loops; at the right size, the picture matches a Sun-centered one exactly.

blocks.html: Ptolemy added two refinements. The Earth is set a little off the center of the deferent (an eccentric). And the epicycle's center moves at a steady angular speed not as seen from the Earth or from the deferent's center but from a third point, the equant, placed on the other side of the center from the Earth. The equant broke the old rule of uniform motion about a circle's center, and many later astronomers disliked it, but it made the predictions much better.

For Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, the line from the epicycle's center to the planet always points the same way as the line from the Earth to the Sun. That is a strong hint that the Sun matters, and it is exactly what a Sun-centered system explains. Copernicus noticed it.

blocks.title: Ptolemy's numbers and the planets' distances
blocks.q: Ptolemy gave Mars an epicycle of radius 39½ on a deferent of radius 60. What is the ratio? Compare it with Earth's distance from the Sun divided by Mars's distance (1 ÷ 1.524).
steps: They agree to within half a percent. Ptolemy's epicycle is, in effect, the Earth's own orbit seen in reverse.

blocks.title: How often does Mars go backward?
blocks.q: Earth goes around the Sun in 1 year, Mars in 1.88 years. How often does Earth overtake Mars, causing a retrograde loop?
steps: Each year Earth gains $1 - \frac{1}{1.88}$ of a lap on Mars.
$1 - 0.532 = 0.468$ of a lap per year.
One full lap takes $1 \div 0.468 \approx 2.14$ years, about 780 days.

blocks.text: Why he kept the Earth still

blocks.html: Ptolemy knew of the idea that the Earth turns. He rejected it with physical arguments: if the Earth spun, clouds and birds and things thrown upward would be left behind toward the west. Answering that objection needed a new physics of motion, which came with Galileo and Newton. Ptolemy was not being stubborn; with the physics of his day, a moving Earth looked impossible.

Believing that by Copernicus's time Ptolemy's system had grown "epicycles on epicycles" to fit the data. The historian Owen Gingerich (1975) showed that the tables in use around 1500 used Ptolemy's original scheme, one epicycle per planet, with no added circles. And Copernicus's own system needed about as many circles as Ptolemy's. The Sun-centered system won because of how it fit together, and later because of Kepler's ellipses, not because it used fewer circles.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the star magnitude scale (modern astronomers still use it, made precise in 1856); much of the trigonometry; the practice of building a model, comparing it with observations and adjusting it.
Changed: the Earth moves (Copernicus, 1543); orbits are ellipses, not circles on circles (Kepler, 1609); all of it follows from gravity (Newton, 1687).

An echo: Kepler's second law makes a planet sweep out equal areas in equal times. Seen from the empty focus of the ellipse, the planet then moves at a nearly steady angular rate, which is just what Ptolemy's equant did.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Did Ptolemy think his circles were real, or only a way to compute? He seems to have thought both mattered. In the Almagest he aims at models that predict; in a later work, the Planetary Hypotheses, he builds them into a physical system of nested shells and estimates the size of the universe. Medieval astronomers argued about whether astronomy describes the world or only "saves the appearances". The same argument came back when Copernicus's book was published with a preface (not by Copernicus) saying the Sun-centered system was only a calculating device.

Historians also debate how much of Ptolemy's star catalog came from Hipparchus, about 265 years earlier. Most think Ptolemy used and updated Hipparchus's work, as he says he did in places; a few have argued he copied more than he admits.

The Almagest was translated into Arabic in the 800s, and astronomers in Baghdad, Damascus, Maragha and Samarkand checked and improved it. Ibn al-Shatir in Damascus (1300s) replaced the equant with extra small circles in a way very like Copernicus's later models. Gerard of Cremona translated it from Arabic into Latin in 1175. Copernicus learned astronomy from it, and his own book follows its plan.

items: If a theory predicts well but is built on a wrong picture, is it a good theory?
Ptolemy's model worked for 1,400 years. Why might people keep a model that works even when it seems strange?
How would you convince someone that the Earth moves, using only what you can see from your backyard?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Act out the Earth and Mars walk. Can you see why Mars seems to go backward?
  2. Ptolemy thought if the Earth spun, things thrown up would land behind us. Why don't they?
  3. Is a good prediction enough, or do we also want a true picture of how things are?
  4. Ptolemy built on Hipparchus, and Copernicus built on Ptolemy. Whose work do you build on when you learn something new?
  5. Look for Mars, Jupiter or Saturn in the night sky (a planet app or almanac can help). Mark its place against the stars over several weeks.

Owen Gingerich, '"Crisis" versus Aesthetic in the Copernican Revolution', Vistas in Astronomy 17 (1975)

blocks.html: A note for parents: Galen's experiments were done on living animals and he describes them plainly. The lesson tells what he found without detail, and the visual is a simple diagram.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Galen was a Greek doctor who lived in the Roman Empire about 1,850 years ago. As a young man he looked after gladiators, the fighters of the Roman games, and later he became doctor to a Roman emperor.

Galen wanted to know how the body does its everyday jobs: how food becomes part of us, how we grow, and how the body gets rid of what it doesn't need. He thought every part of the body has powers (he called them faculties): a power to draw in what it needs, to hold on to it, to change it, and to push out what it doesn't need.
Galen tested his ideas with experiments, which few doctors of his time did. Some of his ideas were later shown to be wrong, but his habit of testing was right.

blocks.name: gb-ureters
blocks.cap: A diagram of Galen's famous test. Tie the tubes from the kidneys and see what happens to the bladder.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Where does the water go? Fold a paper towel into a strip and dip one end into a cup of water. Watch the water climb. A plant does something like this, drawing water up from its roots. Galen thought every part of the body has a power to draw in what it needs. What do you think makes the water climb the paper?

Some people in Galen's day thought the bladder filled up the way a sponge soaks up mist. Galen tied off the tubes that run from the kidneys to the bladder and showed that the bladder stayed empty. Urine is made in the kidneys and flows down those tubes. He was right.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Galen (AD 129–c. 216) was born in Pergamon, a Greek city in what is now western Turkey. He studied medicine there and in Smyrna and Alexandria, served as physician to the gladiators of Pergamon, and moved to Rome in 162, where he became physician to the emperor Marcus Aurelius and later to his son Commodus. He wrote more than any other ancient author whose works survive, on anatomy, medicine, drugs and philosophy.

On the Natural Faculties takes on one question: how does a living body grow, take in food and get rid of waste? In Galen's day two rival schools gave answers he thought wrong. Followers of Erasistratus explained the body by tubes and pressure, like plumbing. Asclepiades explained it by tiny particles and pores, with nothing directing them. Galen argued that living parts have active powers of their own.

head: Faculty
What it does
Galen's example
rows: the kidneys draw urine from the blood
holds it while it is worked on
the stomach closes around food while digesting it
food changed into blood, blood into flesh
pushes out what is unsuitable or finished
blocks.cap: The four faculties that serve nutrition, as Galen describes them.

blocks.html: Galen admits he does not know what a faculty is. A faculty is the name for the unknown cause of an observed effect. He is careful about this: he will not claim more knowledge than he has, but he insists that the effects are real and need a cause.

Asclepiades said urine reaches the bladder as vapor, soaking through. Galen answered with an experiment on a living animal. He tied the ureters, the tubes from the kidneys to the bladder. The bladder stayed empty, and the ureters swelled above the ties. When he loosened them, the bladder filled. Urine comes from the kidneys through the ureters, and nowhere else.

blocks.name: gb-ureters
blocks.cap: Tie one or both ureters. The diagram follows what Galen reported.

blocks.html: A good experiment sets two explanations against each other. If urine soaked in as vapor, tying the ureters would change nothing. If it flows down the ureters, the bladder would stay empty. The bladder stayed empty.

Galen uses the magnet as his favorite example: here is something that plainly attracts at a distance, so why deny that a kidney can attract? The comparison is clever. It is also a warning: naming a power is not the same as explaining it, as later scientists who studied magnets (Gilbert, then Faraday, both on this ladder) would show.

Thinking Galen's anatomy is human anatomy. Dissecting human bodies was not done in his Rome, so he dissected animals, especially apes and pigs, and assumed people were built the same. Some of his descriptions are right for apes but wrong for humans. Andreas Vesalius corrected many of them in 1543 from human dissection.

blocks.text: Blood, the liver and the heart

blocks.html: Galen thought food, once digested, went to the liver, which turned it into blood. Blood then spread through the veins and was used up by the body parts as food, so new blood had to be made all the time. Some blood, he thought, passed from the right side of the heart to the left through tiny pores in the wall between them. This picture lasted 1,400 years, until William Harvey (1628, later on this ladder) measured how much blood the heart pumps and showed it must go round and round.

blocks.title: Harvey's kind of estimate
blocks.q: Suppose the heart pushes out 70 mL of blood with each beat and beats 70 times a minute. How much blood is that in an hour? Could the liver make that much from food?
steps: Per minute: $70 \times 70 = 4{,}900$ mL, about 4.9 liters.
Per hour: $4.9 \times 60 = 294$ liters.
That is far more than the food and drink anyone takes in. The same blood must be used again and again.
blocks.a: About 294 liters an hour, so the blood must circulate.

blocks.text: What later medicine kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: experiment on living things, the idea that each organ has its own function (the root of physiology), and the result that the kidneys make urine. Galen also showed, in another book, that arteries carry blood, not air, as Erasistratus had taught.

Changed: the faculties became processes we can explain: filtration in the kidney, muscular movement of the gut, chemical digestion by enzymes. Galen's anatomy was corrected by Vesalius and his blood by Harvey; the four humors were given up in the 1800s.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Galen believed that nature, which he sometimes calls an artist, does nothing in vain: every part is shaped for its use. He takes this view from Aristotle and Hippocrates. It led him to ask the right question about each organ, what is it for?, and also to accept answers too quickly when an answer seemed fitting. Biologists after Darwin ask the same question in a different way: what did this part do that helped its owners survive and reproduce?

For more than a thousand years, in the Islamic world and in Europe, Galen was "the physician". His books were translated into Syriac, Arabic (by Hunayn ibn Ishaq in the 800s) and Latin. Some later physicians did find errors: Ibn al-Nafis, in Cairo in the 1200s, argued that blood cannot pass through the wall of the heart and must go through the lungs. But most readers took Galen's word over their own eyes. Galen himself had urged doctors to test claims, including old ones. His followers often forgot that part of his teaching.

items: Is it fair to call a power a "faculty" when you don't know what causes it? When does naming help, and when does it hide ignorance?
Galen tested his ideas on animals. People today still argue about when experiments on animals are justified; what do you think the main arguments are on each side?
Why do people go on trusting a famous expert even after some of their claims are shown to be wrong?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Galen tested two ideas against each other with one experiment. Can you think of an experiment that would decide between two ideas you have heard?
  2. Galen thought every part of the body has a job. Pick a part of your body and say what you think its job is.
  3. Why might it be hard to correct a famous teacher's mistake, even many years later?
  4. Galen admitted he didn't know what a faculty was. When is it good to say "I don't know"?
  5. Plants and animals both grow and take in food. What can animals do that plants can't, according to Galen?
